More than US$20 billion has been pledged, including US$14.3 billion at the One Planet Summit in January 2021, which launched the Great Green Wall Accelerator. Disbursement has lagged: countries reported receiving only US$149 million between 2011 and 2019, and by March 2023 only US$2.5 billion of the 2021 pledge had been disbursed. The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) estimated that the 2030 target needs about US$4.3 billion a year.

## What Makes It New

It is a pan-African, multi-country restoration effort organised around one geographic belt, combining land restoration with jobs and climate goals, and it shifted from a tree-planting concept to landscape-scale restoration.

## Measuring Impact

The UNCCD's first status report, in 2020, found that about 20 million hectares were restored between 2007 and 2018, but only about 4% of the demarcated intervention zone; the rest lay elsewhere in participating countries, including about 12 million hectares in Ethiopia. It counted more than 350,000 jobs and around US$90 million in revenue. A field and satellite study of 36 planted plots in Senegal, covering about 18,000 hectares, found only one plot greener than expected from rainfall alone, indicating little ecological effect there. Results are weak relative to targets, vary widely by country, and direct evidence on dust reduction is lacking.

## Risks & Mitigation

Reported problems include slow, fragmented funding, weak monitoring, low survival of unirrigated seedlings, livestock damage where fencing is poorly maintained, and insecurity that has halted aid and destabilised sites in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. Some countries lacked an agency able to receive funds, and critics have called the approach top-down. The UNCCD named financing, governance and monitoring as priorities, and the Accelerator was launched to scale up funding.

name: Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) for Delhi-NCR
place: Delhi and National Capital Region, India
description:
## One-Sentence Summary

The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) is a set of emergency anti-pollution measures for Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR) that are switched on in stages as the Air Quality Index (AQI) worsens; it was first notified by India's environment ministry in 2017 and revised by the Commission for Air Quality Management in 2022.

## Problem

Delhi recorded an annual average PM10 of 197 µg/m³ in 2025, nearly three times the national standard of 60. Pollution peaks in autumn and winter, when weak winds combine with vehicle exhaust, construction and road dust, crop-residue burning and household and waste burning.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases

The plan aims to protect residents of Delhi and surrounding NCR districts during pollution episodes, especially children, older people and people with respiratory disease. Central, state and municipal agencies and police use it to decide which restrictions apply each day.

## Solution / Service Overview

Since October 2022 GRAP has four cumulative stages: Stage I (AQI 201–300), Stage II (301–400), Stage III (401–450) and Stage IV (above 450). Lower stages cover dust control, road sweeping, fines for open burning and reliable electricity to cut diesel generator use. Stage III adds a ban on most construction and allows curbs on older petrol and diesel cars. Stage IV halts construction, bans entry of most trucks, and allows school closures, work-from-home orders and odd-even driving. Forecasts from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) inform decisions.

## Delivery Model

GRAP arose from Supreme Court proceedings in the M.C. Mehta case and was first implemented through the court-mandated Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority. The Commission for Air Quality Management, a statutory body, now invokes stages and directs agencies to enforce them. Revisions in December 2024 and November 2025 moved several measures to earlier stages.

## Funding & Sustainability

GRAP has no dedicated budget and relies on existing agencies; much of its cost falls on businesses and workers. The Supreme Court directed NCR states to use construction-worker welfare cess funds to pay subsistence allowances to workers idled by construction bans.

## What Makes It New

It ties pre-agreed restrictions to AQI bands so action follows automatically as pollution rises, across several state jurisdictions within one airshed.

## Measuring Impact

Independent evaluation is limited. A joint study by IITM and the Commission, reported in 2025, estimated that GRAP lowered PM2.5 by 2 to 42 µg/m³ depending on the stage, that Delhi would otherwise have had about 60% more hours of severe air quality, and that 177 to 297 short-term deaths may have been averted. This is a modelling estimate produced partly by the implementing body. Winter air quality remains very poor, and independent experts say the plan has not significantly reduced Delhi's overall pollution.

## Risks & Mitigation

Experts describe GRAP as a reactive emergency tool that treats symptoms rather than sources, relies on an outdated emissions inventory and lacks a mechanism to check whether measures cut emissions across the NCR. Enforcement has been uneven: in December 2024 the Supreme Court found that Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh had not shown payment of allowances to any construction worker idled by Stage IV, and summoned their chief secretaries. The Commission has responded by moving measures to earlier stages and promising stricter enforcement of existing norms.

name: Fine Dust Seasonal Management System (December–March)
description:
## One-Sentence Summary

South Korea's Fine Dust Seasonal Management System applies extra emission controls every year from December to March, first in winter 2019–20, idling coal power plants, restricting the most polluting vehicles and tightening industrial controls when fine particulate pollution is worst.

## Problem

Fine particulate (PM2.5) concentrations in South Korea peak between December and March, when stagnant weather and heating demand combine with emissions from coal power, steel and other industry and diesel vehicles, plus pollution transported from China. Severe episodes in early 2019 caused strong public concern.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases

The system protects the national population, especially in the Seoul metropolitan area and in provinces such as South Chungcheong where coal plants and steel mills are concentrated. It is applied by ministries, power companies and local governments.

## Solution / Service Overview

The National Council on Climate and Air Quality proposed the system in September 2019, aiming to cut fine dust by at least 20% from December to March. For the first season, 14 of about 60 coal plants were scheduled to be idled from December to February and up to 27 in March; in the second, 9 to 16 were to be idled, with the rest capped at 80% of capacity. Cities restrict "grade 5" vehicles, mainly diesel cars made before July 2002 and petrol cars made before 1987. Seoul bans them on weekdays from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., with fines of up to 100,000 won per day and exemptions for filter-equipped, emergency and low-income households' vehicles.

## Delivery Model

A March 2020 amendment to the Special Act on the Reduction and Management of Fine Dust gave the system a legal basis: from 1 December to 31 March the environment minister can ask agencies to adjust emitting facilities' operating rates and restrict ships, and local leaders can restrict old vehicles by ordinance. It is repeated each winter.

## Funding & Sustainability

Costs fall mainly on the power sector, which replaces coal generation, and on owners of older vehicles. Scrapping and retrofitting were promoted alongside the bans; about 113,000 grade 5 vehicles were scrapped or fitted with emission-reduction devices in the first season.

## What Makes It New

Rather than reacting only to daily alerts, it applies planned season-long controls when pollution is predictably worst, including South Korea's first winter shutdowns of coal plants.

## Measuring Impact

The Ministry of Environment estimated that the first season (December 2019 to March 2020) cut the national average PM2.5 concentration by about 1.9 µg/m³. Days with PM2.5 at or above 36 µg/m³ fell by two on average nationally and by up to nine in South Chungcheong. Favourable weather was estimated to have lowered concentrations by about 3 µg/m³, and reduced activity during COVID-19 also contributed, so the policy explains only part of the improvement. Seoul later reported a 26% year-on-year fall in one season, but its winter concentrations still exceed the annual average.

## Risks & Mitigation

Attribution is difficult because weather, COVID-19 and Chinese emission controls overlap with the policy; officials said China's contribution could not be measured precisely. Vehicle bans burden owners of older cars, hence the exemptions. Because the measures are temporary, they are paired with longer-term steps such as Seoul's ban on grade 4 diesel vehicles in its centre from 2025.

name: Breathe London low-cost air quality sensor network
description:
## One-Sentence Summary

Breathe London is a city-wide network of low-cost air quality sensors, piloted from 2018 and expanded with Greater London Authority funding from 2021, that publishes street-level nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate data for the public, boroughs and community groups.

## Problem

London's official reference monitors are accurate but expensive and relatively sparse, so many neighbourhoods, schools and hospitals had no local measurements. Residents and boroughs lacked street-level data to find pollution hotspots, target local action or involve communities that had taken little part in clean-air programmes.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases

Users include London boroughs, schools, hospitals, community groups, charities and residents. The expanded network prioritised low-income and Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities, which City Hall said had been less engaged in environmental programmes. Uses include assessing local schemes such as School Streets, informing residents and supporting campaigns.

## Solution / Service Overview

The two-year pilot, from late 2018, tested about 100 fixed low-cost sensors, sensors on Google Street View cars, wearable sensors on children's school journeys and an evaluation of School Streets. In December 2020 the Mayor announced a new network of more than 100 sensors measuring nitrogen dioxide and PM2.5 at priority sites such as schools and hospitals. Data appear on a public map, and groups can "buy in" to host extra sensors at reduced cost. The sensor supplier reports more than 400 sensors.

## Delivery Model

The pilot was led by Environmental Defense Fund Europe. The expanded network is delivered by Imperial College London's Environmental Research Group through Imperial Projects, with City Hall as the main funder, and sensors are calibrated against nearby reference monitors.

## Funding & Sustainability

The pilot was funded by the Children's Investment Fund Foundation and the Clean Air Fund. The Mayor committed £750,000 over four years to the follow-on network, and Bloomberg Philanthropies supported outreach to less-engaged communities. Further growth relies on paid hosting by boroughs, businesses and community groups.

## What Makes It New

Its funders described the pilot as a global first in the scale of low-cost sensor trials across a city, combining fixed, mobile and wearable monitoring. The model became a template for the C40 Breathe Cities programme.

## Measuring Impact

Breathe London is an information service, and there is no evidence that it reduced pollution by itself. Its main measured outcome is data quality. A peer-reviewed evaluation of 100 nitrogen dioxide sensors over about two years found average uncertainty of about 35% after calibration and good tracking of reference measurements (median R² of 0.79); the network reproduced trends, daily and weekly patterns and a December 2019 pollution episode. However, sensors read high in warm weather, overstating daytime concentrations by about 40% in July 2019, and had multi-week periods of poor performance. Evidence on how the data changed behaviour or policy is largely qualitative.

## Risks & Mitigation

Low-cost sensors cannot replace reference monitors, which alone are used to check compliance with legal limits, and uncorrected data can mislead users far from reference sites. The project used co-location with reference instruments, travelling transfer-standard units and network calibration, and its evaluators recommend keeping at least one reliable reference instrument where coverage is sparse. The network depends on time-limited grants and paid hosting.

name: US EPA AirNow and the Air Quality Index (AQI) public information and alert system
description:
## One-Sentence Summary

AirNow is the United States' national system, run by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) with partner agencies since 1998, that gathers real-time air quality measurements and forecasts and communicates them to the public through the colour-coded Air Quality Index (AQI).

## Problem

Ozone and fine particle levels vary daily and can harm health on bad days, but in the mid-1990s data from state and local monitors were not available to the public in real time or in an understandable form. People with asthma or heart disease, children and older adults had no simple way to know when to limit outdoor exposure.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases

The public and sensitive groups use AirNow to plan outdoor activity. Schools, health professionals, forecasters and media use it to issue warnings, and agencies use it for forecasting and wildfire smoke response.

## Solution / Service Overview

The AQI converts concentrations of five pollutants regulated under the Clean Air Act (ground-level ozone, particle pollution, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide) into a scale where 100 generally corresponds to the short-term national standard. Six colour-coded categories run from green ("good", 0–50) to maroon ("hazardous", 301 and above), each with health guidance. AirNow publishes current conditions, daily forecasts, maps, an email alert service called EnviroFlash, apps, and a Fire and Smoke Map developed with the US Forest Service that also uses low-cost sensor data. It also shows data for Canada and Mexico.

## Delivery Model

State, local and tribal agencies operate monitors and send data hourly to a central data management centre, which quality-checks and distributes them; state and local agencies issue official forecasts. Partners include the EPA, NOAA, the National Park Service, NASA and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A contractor has operated the data centre since 2002.

## Funding & Sustainability

AirNow grew from a 1997 regional ozone-mapping system funded by north-eastern state and regional air organisations, and expanded nationally with federal funding from the EMPACT initiative, which also helped states buy equipment. It builds on monitoring networks that agencies already run for regulatory purposes.

## What Makes It New

It created a single national, near-real-time public channel for regulatory monitoring data, using one index shared by agencies and the media. An international version was first deployed in Shanghai for the 2010 World Expo.

## Measuring Impact

AirNow's reach is wide: it reports real-time conditions for more than 400 US cities using data from over 150 agencies. Direct evidence of health benefits is limited. Research on smog alerts in Southern California found that people reduced discretionary outdoor activities on alert days, but that this response had largely disappeared by the second consecutive alert day. AirNow does not itself reduce emissions, and how far its information improves health outcomes has not been established.

## Risks & Mitigation

Index categories depend on the underlying standards. In May 2024 the EPA lowered the upper limit of "good" for PM2.5 from 12 to 9 µg/m³, citing health risks at low levels, and lowered the "very unhealthy" and "hazardous" breakpoints, so the same concentration now gives a higher index value. Regulatory monitors are sparse in some areas, which the Fire and Smoke Map partly addresses with low-cost sensors. Public response weakens during multi-day episodes.

name: California Smog Check vehicle inspection and maintenance programme (BAR with CARB)
description:
## One-Sentence Summary

California's Smog Check is a vehicle emissions inspection and maintenance programme, administered by the Bureau of Automotive Repair (BAR) since 1984 with the California Air Resources Board (CARB) and the Department of Motor Vehicles, that requires most cars to pass an emissions inspection every two years and on change of ownership.

## Problem

Motor vehicles are a major source of the gases that form ozone smog in California. Emission controls deteriorate, fail or are tampered with, so a minority of poorly maintained, mostly older vehicles emit far more than their certified levels.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases

The programme benefits residents of air basins with serious ozone problems, such as Los Angeles, Sacramento and the Central Valley, where stricter "enhanced" rules apply. It applies to vehicle owners and licensed private stations.

## Solution / Service Overview

California adopted the programme under 1982 legislation, and BAR began administering it in 1984. Responding to US EPA requirements, an enhanced programme with loaded dynamometer testing began in 1998 in the most polluted areas. Since 2013, model-year 2000 and newer vehicles are checked mainly through on-board diagnostics, while 1976–1999 vehicles get tailpipe tests. Vehicles eight model years old or newer skip biennial tests but pay an abatement fee. Failing vehicles must be repaired before registration renewal. A Consumer Assistance Program offers eligible owners repair help or payment to retire a vehicle.

## Delivery Model

Inspections are done by privately owned, BAR-licensed stations. Since 2013 a voluntary STAR certification has directed higher-risk vehicles to better-performing stations; in 2023, 48% of stations were STAR-certified and performed 83% of tests. BAR and the California Highway Patrol run voluntary roadside tests to audit results, and BAR can suspend or revoke station licences.

## Funding & Sustainability

Motorists pay for inspections and repairs at private stations, and owners of newer exempt vehicles pay the abatement fee. In 2020 the maximum state contribution to repairs for eligible consumers rose from $500 to $1,200.

## What Makes It New

It combines a decentralised network of private stations with data-driven oversight: roadside audit testing, station performance scores used to route vehicles, and on-board diagnostic checks for newer cars.

## Measuring Impact

A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study estimated that in 1999 the programme cut tailpipe hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides by about 97, 1,690 and 81 tons per day, with wide uncertainty (60–91 tons per day for nitrogen oxides); repairs after failed tests delivered most of the benefit. A persistent gap remains: in 2022–23 about 14% of vehicles failed a roadside test within a year of their Smog Check, including 14% of those that had passed. BAR and CARB estimated that an extra 48 tons per day of reactive organic gases and nitrogen oxides could have been removed in 2023 if all stations performed as well as the best.

## Risks & Mitigation

Fraud recurs, including "clean piping" (testing a sample from a clean car), its diagnostic equivalent "clean plugging" and registration fraud, and cases are slow to pursue. The US EPA has argued that testing and repairing at the same station creates a conflict of interest. Stricter tests caused many older vehicles to fail, raising owners' costs. Mitigations include STAR certification, roadside auditing and repair and retirement assistance.

name: Santiago Atmospheric Prevention and Decontamination Plan (PPDA)
description:
## One-Sentence Summary

Santiago de Chile's Atmospheric Prevention and Decontamination Plan (PPDA) is a legally binding plan for the Metropolitan Region, first adopted in 1997 after the area was declared saturated with several pollutants, that combines permanent controls on transport, industry and home heating with emergency measures on high-pollution winter days.

## Problem

Santiago lies in a basin with poor winter ventilation, and in the 1990s it had very high levels of particulate matter, ozone and carbon monoxide. Main sources included buses and cars, industry and residential wood burning, and winter fine particle levels are typically about double summer levels.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases

The plan protects residents of the Metropolitan Region, especially north-western districts most affected by particulate matter and eastern and central districts most affected by ozone. It regulates drivers, transport operators, industry, construction and households.

## Solution / Service Overview

A 1996 decree declared Santiago saturated with ozone, particulate matter and carbon monoxide. The 1997 plan set out 104 actions for 29 institutions over a planned 14 years. It was revised in 2004, as urban growth and a rising vehicle fleet threatened progress, and again in 2017. Measures have included natural gas and cleaner fuels, catalytic-converter cars, licence-plate driving restrictions, a ban on wood-burning heaters across Santiago province, industrial emission-reduction plans targeting a 30% particulate cut by 2027, and electric buses. From May to August, declared alerts, pre-emergencies and emergencies trigger extra driving restrictions and industrial shutdowns.

## Delivery Model

The national environmental authority, originally CONAMA and now the Ministry of the Environment, prepares the plan, issued as a decree. Regional health, transport and environmental agencies, the police and the Superintendency of the Environment inspect vehicles, homes and factories. Plans must be reviewed every five years and updated every ten.

## Funding & Sustainability

Measures are funded through public budgets and obligations on emitters, including industrial reduction plans and an emissions compensation programme that has replaced more than 12,000 wood heaters in rural parts of the region. Periodic legal revision has kept the plan in force for nearly three decades.

## What Makes It New

It ties a formal saturation declaration to a binding multi-sector plan with mandatory periodic revision, paired with a structured winter episode system.

## Measuring Impact

Annual PM2.5 fell from about 69 µg/m³ in 1989 to 20 µg/m³ in 2020, a 71% reduction, and annual PM10 fell from 97 µg/m³ in 1997 to 68 in 2004. Progress has not been steady. An analysis of the 2005 audit found that reductions stalled after 2000, with days exceeding the daily PM10 standard rising from 49 in 2001 to 67 in 2003, and no decline in ozone. The four winters to 2021 had 127 critical episodes and no emergencies, against 170 episodes and seven emergencies in the previous four, and 2024 was reported as the third-best year since the plan began. Dry winters give markedly worse results.

## Risks & Mitigation

Reported problems include weak enforcement of wood-burning bans and smoky-vehicle rules, delays in approving industrial reduction plans, a growing car fleet and too few monitoring stations in outlying towns. Earlier, cuts in Argentine natural gas pushed some sources back to diesel, and political priority has varied. The Superintendency raised its inspections from about 108 in 2023 to over 350 in 2024.

name: Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 (with the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution as context)
description:
## One-Sentence Summary

Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 makes companies, including foreign ones, criminally and civilly liable if fires on land they own or occupy outside Singapore cause or contribute to unhealthy haze in Singapore, complementing the regional ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

## Problem

Fires used to clear land for palm oil and pulp and paper plantations in Indonesia repeatedly send smoke haze across Singapore. The ASEAN haze agreement, signed in 2002, did not stop haze returning almost every year from 2004 to 2010 and from 2013 to 2015; Indonesia, the main source, ratified it last, in 2014. Critics call the agreement vague and lacking enforcement.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases

The law aims to protect Singapore's population from haze and to deter plantation companies, their Singapore-linked parents and executives from using fire. The National Environment Agency (NEA) uses it to demand action during episodes and to investigate companies.

## Solution / Service Overview

Parliament passed the Act on 5 August 2014. It covers conduct outside Singapore that causes or contributes to haze in Singapore. Companies can be fined up to S$100,000 for each day they contribute to unhealthy haze, to a maximum of S$2 million, and the Act also creates civil liability. The NEA can issue preventive measure notices requiring a company to deploy firefighters, stop burning and submit fire-control plans, and can demand information from related Singapore entities. Evidentiary presumptions, such as inferring land control from maps and records, can be rebutted.

## Delivery Model

The NEA enforces the Act. Notices can be served on officers of foreign companies when they are in Singapore, with immigration authorities helping to track their entry. Evidence relies largely on satellite images, concession maps and weather data, because investigators cannot freely work in Indonesia.

## Funding & Sustainability

The Act is a liability law rather than a spending programme, enforced by the NEA. Its deterrent effect depends on reputational pressure, Singapore-linked assets, market access and action against executives entering Singapore, rather than on large fines.

## What Makes It New

The government described it as introducing novel elements into law: criminal and civil liability applied extraterritorially to companies for air pollution caused in another country, including firms without assets or presence in Singapore.

## Measuring Impact

Measured results are weak. In September 2015, when the three-hour Pollutant Standards Index reached 341 and all primary and secondary schools closed, the NEA served preventive notices on four Indonesian companies, then a fifth, plus an information notice on a Singapore-based pulp and paper group. Singapore investigated several Indonesian companies in 2016, but legal commentary reports no convictions under the Act. Haze reached unhealthy levels again in September 2019, for the first time since 2016, during a dry year with widespread fires in Sumatra. Changes in haze frequency cannot be attributed to the Act because weather strongly drives fire activity.

## Risks & Mitigation

Indonesia objected to the law's extraterritorial reach and threatened to review environmental cooperation. Gathering evidence inside Indonesia is difficult, overlapping land-use maps complicate identifying responsible companies, and some scholars question the evidentiary presumptions. Members of Parliament warned that the S$2 million cap could be a "slap on the wrist" for large firms; the government said the Act would be reviewed once in effect.
